methodological_questions: temporal ordering of play types within a possession
possession boundary definition and its interaction with play-type labels
accuracy and calibration of play-type labels, especially DRIVE and PNR
confounding by game situation, defensive scheme, and offensive context
sample size and sparsity of teammate-drive-then-PNR sequences
selection bias in which drives precede PNR actions

historical_evidence.finding: Defensive scheme change within game and across games using outcome-inferred labels produced near-uniform transition matrices consistent with label noise. The inferred label cannot separate real defensive adjustment from offense executing differently.

Play-type label backfill verification failed: PNR share 28.7% (outside 20-28% band), PULL_UP 7.9% fail, many 2024-25 teams near 0% for PULL_UP, 82.8% of PNR labels proxy-calibrated. Overall verification FAIL.
Observable on-ball defensive scheme labels from NBA matchup/PBP fields yielded confident label rates of only 14.9% and 3.3% for on-ball possessions, and the switches_on field was not populated.

Play-type labeling audit: 36% of OTHER possessions end in fouls, inflating OTHER PPP; DRIVE sits 12 percentage points below the foul benchmark (foul leakage); PNR shows 22% foul rate; only 0.7% of possessions map to a real play type via initiation_type.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Backfilled play-type label verification, including PNR labels
failed_approaches.why: PNR label share outside expected band and 82.8% proxy calibration; failure mechanism: label error (C_artifact).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Using DRIVE labels as a clean play-type indicator
failed_approaches.why: DRIVE suffers from foul leakage, distorting PPP and likely missing drive events that end in fouls; failure mechanism: artifact (C_artifact).

evidence_establishes: DRIVE labels exhibit systematic foul leakage, missing drives that end in fouls and biasing DRIVE PPP estimates.
PNR labels are heavily proxy-calibrated (82.8%) and fail league-distribution and team-identity checks in backfill verification.
Play-type labeling quality in the current pipeline is insufficient for analyses relying on accurate identification and sequencing of play types.
evidence_does_not_establish: The precise magnitude or direction of bias in estimating the effect of a preceding teammate drive on PNR PPP.
Whether the possession-level graph database correctly captures the temporal ordering of play types when labels themselves may be missing or incorrect.
What fraction of actual PNR possessions contain a preceding teammate drive, or whether such sequences have enough sample for a powered test.
own_inferences: The combination of DRIVE foul leakage and PNR proxy calibration makes it highly likely that any observed relationship between a preceding drive and PNR PPP is an artifact of systematic mislabeling rather than a true effect.

Even if an effect were detected, the current label quality would preclude a causal interpretation, as both the exposure (preceding drive) and the outcome (PNR PPP) rely on labels with known, nontrivial error.
The research question is effectively untestable with the current data until the underlying play-type labeling pipeline is substantially improved and validated.
uncertainties: The exact error rate of drive and PNR labels in the specific dataset version available on 2026-06-14 is not given; only known failures from earlier verifications.
The graph database’s handling of possession boundaries when fouls occur may further distort the sequence identification.
Potential confounders (defensive matchup, game situation, rest) are not assessed in the historical records and could add bias even with perfect labels.

historical_effect.explanation: Without historical evidence, one might have assumed the play-type labels were sufficiently reliable for a sequence analysis. The retrieved records show that PNR labels fail verification and DRIVE labels suffer from foul leakage, both of which directly undermine the identification of the exposure and outcome. This evidence moves the decision from a tentative ‘proceed’ to ‘do_not_proceed’ unless the labeling pipeline is rebuilt and revalidated.

blocking_constraints.text: PNR labels are 82.8% proxy-calibrated and fail share checks; DRIVE labels exhibit foul leakage. The sequence identification requires both labels to be accurate.
The play-type labeling pipeline has documented reliability failures, making the measurement of both exposure and outcome untrustworthy.
The effective sample of possessions with a correctly labeled preceding teammate drive and a correctly labeled PNR may be too small for adequate power, even if label errors could be ignored.

prior_work.summary: No prior study directly tested whether a teammate drive preceding a PNR raises PNR PPP. However, verification and audit studies show that the underlying play-type labels (PNR, DRIVE) contain serious errors that would preclude a valid test of this question.

risks.text: PNR label proxy calibration and share failure (SF-APPA-030); DRIVE label foul leakage (SF-CHT-025) distort both the exposure and outcome variables.
The tool chain that assigns play types to possession segments has documented unreliability; the confidence in any derived sequence variable is low.
If drives and PNRs are mislabeled or missed, the number of qualifying possessions may be insufficient to detect a plausible effect size.

Game situation, defensive matchups, offensive set play design, and fatigue could all influence both the likelihood of a preceding drive and the PNR outcome, requiring extensive covariate control that may still leave residual confounding.
If the labeling algorithm uses future information to classify play types (e.g., shot outcome), the temporal ordering of drive and PNR could be compromised.

design.estimand: The causal effect of a correctly labeled teammate drive action occurring in a possession prior to a correctly labeled pick-and-roll on the points per possession (PPP) of the PNR, relative to PNR possessions with no preceding teammate drive.
design.unit: Individual possession with an identified PNR action.
design.sample: All regular-season and playoff possessions from NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26 seasons where a PNR is recorded in the graph database, excluding those with missing play-type labels or ambiguous possession boundaries.
design.power: Not estimable with current label quality; would require a label validation study to quantify effective sample size and minimum detectable effect.
design.controls: Score margin (period-adjusted), time remaining in shot clock, offensive team identity, defensive team identity, opponent defensive scheme (if available), home/away, rest days, lineup-based offensive rating.
design.falsification: Compare estimated effect for possessions where PNR label confidence is high (non-proxy-calibrated) vs. low; test for effect before and after a play-type labeling improvement. A zero or unstable effect in the high-confidence subset would indicate label-driven artifact.
design.multiplicity: Single hypothesis test; no multiple comparisons correction needed unless extended to other play-type sequences.
design.decision_rule: Bayesian hierarchical model with partial pooling across teams and shrinkage on possession-level effects, reporting posterior probability of a positive effect. Classical approach: regression with clustered standard errors at team level, α=0.05 (two-sided).
design.data_version: NBA stats API per-game files and derived graph database as of 2026-06-14.

Research question (as posed on 2026-06-14, in the area of play-type labeling and data quality):
Any teammate DRIVE preceding a PNR raises PNR PPP.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)

Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

First, understand the research question: It's about the effect of a teammate's drive action occurring before a pick-and-roll (PNR) on the pick-and-roll's points per possession (PPP). The data includes play-by-play with action types and sub-types, so we can identify drive and PNR actions. The question is about sequencing: a drive by a teammate (not the PNR ball-handler) preceding a PNR. The outcome is PNR PPP.

We need to identify research concepts and methodological questions. Research concepts: "teammate drive", "pick and roll", "PNR PPP", "play sequencing", "possession outcomes". Methodological questions might involve: defining "preceding" (time window, same possession?), handling of multiple drives, correlation vs causation, sample size, play-type labeling reliability, leakage (e.g., using future info to define preceding), possession boundaries, handling of turnovers, etc.

Given the task, we must call retrieve_history with research_concepts and methodological_questions, and a query summarizing. The output should be a JSON object calling the tool.

Let's craft the args. I'll list research_concepts like "teammate drive", "pick and roll", "PNR efficiency", "play sequencing", "possession prior actions". Methodological_questions: "temporal ordering of play types", "possession boundary definition", "play-type labeling accuracy", "confounding by game situation", "sample size and sparsity of drive-then-PNR sequences", "selection bias in drives that lead to PNR". The query: "Any teammate DRIVE preceding a PNR raises PNR PPP."

So:
{
  "action": "tool",
  "tool": "retrieve_history",
  "args": {
    "research_concepts": ["teammate drive", "pick and roll", "PNR efficiency", "play sequencing", "prior actions in possession"],
    "methodological_questions": ["temporal ordering of play types", "possession boundary definition", "play-type labeling accuracy", "confounding by game situation", "sample size and sparsity", "selection bias"],
    "query": "Any teammate DRIVE preceding a PNR raises PNR PPP."
  }
}

We are in Stage 2. We received retrieval results with 4 study-family records: FAM:SF-APPA-005, FAM:SF-APPA-030, FAM:SF-APPS-058, FAM:SF-CHT-025. We need to summarize relevant historical findings and failed approaches, assess what evidence establishes and does not establish, own inferences, uncertainties, historical effect on decision, testability, prior work, risks, predicted outcome, decision, and design.

First, understand the research question: "Any teammate DRIVE preceding a PNR raises PNR PPP." That is, in a possession, if a teammate (not the ball-handler) had a drive action (play type DRIVE) before a pick-and-roll (PNR) occurs in the same possession, does that increase the points per possession (PPP) of the PNR? The data: per-game play-by-play, derived play-type possession records in a graph database. So they have play-type labels (DRIVE, PNR, etc.) and possession-level points. The question is about a sequential relationship: a drive by a teammate before a PNR in the same possession and its effect on the PNR's efficiency.

Relevant historical evidence:
- FAM:SF-APPA-005: about defensive scheme change using inferred labels. Status: untestable. Finding: transition matrices near-uniform, consistent with label noise. Limitation: label error. This is about defensive scheme labels being unreliable when inferred backwards from opponent play-type PPP. It suggests label noise in play-type labels, but not directly about DRIVE or PNR labels.
- FAM:SF-APPA-030: Play-type label backfill verification. Status: inconclusive, but found many failures: PNR share 28.7% (outside band), many teams PULL_UP near 0%, 82.8% of PNR labels proxy_calibrated. Risk: LABEL_ERROR. That's critical: PNR labels themselves are heavily proxy-calibrated and fail verification. This would directly affect a study using PNR labels.
- FAM:SF-APPS-058: On-ball defensive scheme labels, low coverage, label error, sample size. Not directly about play-type labels but about defensive scheme labels from matchup/PBP fields.
- FAM:SF-CHT-025: Play-type labeling audit: OTHER/DRIVE foul leakage. DRIVE shows 12pp below foul benchmark (foul leakage), meaning DRIVE labels might be under-assigned when a foul occurs? Also, initiation_type maps only 0.7% of possessions to a play type. So DRIVE labels suffer from foul leakage artifact. This suggests that when a drive results in a foul, it might not be labeled as DRIVE or the possession might be classified differently, thus DRIVE PPP is distorted. For the question, "teammate DRIVE preceding a PNR" requires identifying DRIVE actions and PNR actions in the same possession. If DRIVE labels are noisy and missing foul-related drives, that would affect the ability to detect a preceding drive. Also, PNR labels have issues per SF-APPA-030.

Thus, the historical evidence strongly suggests that play-type labels are problematic, especially PNR (proxy_calibrated, share failures) and DRIVE (foul leakage). Also, the possession-level linkage might have issues (initiation_type maps only 0.7%). The graph database is built from play-by-play, but the labeling process is flawed. These records indicate that any analysis relying on these labels is at high risk of artifact due to label error.

Now, fill out the output schema.

First, research_concepts: list concepts from the question: teammate drive, pick-and-roll, PNR efficiency, play sequencing, prior actions in possession.

methodological_questions: temporal ordering, possession boundary definition, play-type labeling accuracy, confounding by game situation, sample size and sparsity, selection bias (like when drives occur before PNR might be non-random).

historical_evidence: list each record with id, status, finding. We'll use the auto_outcome_status field but need to match the schema's requirement: "status_as_recorded: outcome status exactly as stated in the record". The records have auto_outcome_status: untestable, inconclusive, untestable, artifact. So we'll list:
- FAM:SF-APPA-005: untestable, finding from observed_result and observed_failure_evidence.
- FAM:SF-APPA-030: inconclusive, but with failure evidence.
- FAM:SF-APPS-058: untestable.
- FAM:SF-CHT-025: artifact.

failed_approaches: For this research question, what approaches might fail? The records themselves aren't directly testing the same question, but they reveal failures in label reliability. So we can list them: SF-APPA-030 (play-type label backfill verification failed for PNR), SF-CHT-025 (DRIVE foul leakage artifact). Also SF-APPA-005: using outcome-inferred labels leads to noise. SF-APPS-058: defensive label coverage too low.

evidence_establishes: what does it establish? That the play-type labeling pipeline has known errors: PNR labels are heavily proxy-calibrated (82.8%), fail team-identity checks; DRIVE labels suffer from foul leakage; initiation_type mapping is sparse (0.7%). These issues make it unlikely that a clean test of "DRIVE preceding PNR" can be conducted because both labels are unreliable. Also, there is evidence of label noise leading to near-uniform transition matrices (SF-APPA-005), although that's about defensive scheme labels, it indicates a broader problem with label inference.

evidence_does_not_establish: It does not directly quantify the error rate for sequence labeling (whether a DRIVE is correctly identified as occurring before a PNR in the same possession) or the bias in estimating the effect on PNR PPP. Also, it doesn't address confounders like game situation. So we can't say the effect is zero or not.

own_inferences: Given the label errors, any estimated effect of a preceding drive on PNR PPP will likely be biased toward zero or produce spurious results. Because DRIVE labels miss foul-ending drives (which might be high-efficiency plays), the sample of possessions with a DRIVE preceding a PNR might be non-representative. Also, PNR labels are proxy-calibrated, meaning many PNRs might be mislabeled. These issues combine to make the test unreliable. Even if a pattern is found, it could be an artifact of labeling. Therefore, the question is likely untestable with current data.

uncertainties: The exact accuracy of sequence labeling in the graph database is unknown. The sample size might be sufficient if label errors are random, but they appear systematic. There's also uncertainty about how the possession boundaries are defined (does a drive that leads to a foul count as a separate possession?).

historical_effect: The historical evidence changes the decision because without it, one might assume the labels are adequate. The evidence shows prior failures that directly undermine the study. So changed_decision: yes, and explanation: The retrieved records demonstrate that both DRIVE and PNR labels have severe validation failures (foul leakage, proxy calibration, share failures). These failures would prevent a valid test of the question, so the decision moves from "proceed" to "do_not_proceed" unless substantial label improvements are made.

testability: p_testable: very low, maybe 0.1. Blocking constraints: LABEL_ERROR, SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER (specific events rare? but not directly established, but possible), MEASURE_RELIABILITY. So list blocking constraints with codes.

prior_work: already_answered: No. The question hasn't been directly tested. But the prior work shows the labels are unreliable, making the question unanswerable. So "no" or "unknown"? The schema says: "Whether retrieved earlier work already answered substantially the same question." No, it didn't. So "no". cited: list identifiers of records we rely on for that determination: SF-APPA-030 and SF-CHT-025 directly relevant to label quality, SF-APPA-005 about label noise.

risks: List risks: LABEL_ERROR (PNR proxy calibration, DRIVE foul leakage), MEASURE_RELIABILITY (labels unreliable), SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER (maybe few possessions have a teammate drive followed by a PNR, but not established; but could be a risk), CONFOUNDING (game situation, defense, fatigue). Also possibly LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD if play-type labeling uses future information to classify, but we don't know. However, based on evidence, LABEL_ERROR is the primary. Also MULTIPLE_TESTING if we test many sequences, but we're focusing on one. So primary risks: LABEL_ERROR, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, maybe SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, CONFOUNDING.

predicted_outcome: probabilities. Given severe label issues, the test would likely be untestable or artifact. So untestable: 0.6, artifact: 0.3, uncertain: 0.1, supported/rejected negligible. I'll assign: supported: 0.0, rejected: 0.0, untestable: 0.7, artifact: 0.2, uncertain: 0.1.

decision: do_not_proceed.

design: Even though not proceeding, we need a minimum viable test design. Estimand: The causal effect of a teammate drive action occurring in a possession prior to a pick-and-roll on the points per possession from that PNR, compared to possessions with a PNR but no preceding teammate drive. Unit: individual PNR possession. Sample: All possessions from NBA 2022-23 to 2025-26 regular seasons and playoffs where a PNR is identified, with a binary indicator for whether a teammate drive preceded it. Power: not applicable because labels are unreliable. Controls: game situation (score margin, period, time remaining), offensive lineup, defensive team, possibly prior play types. Falsification: test whether the effect differs by label quality proxy (e.g., proxy-calibrated vs non-calibrated PNR labels if available). Multiplicity: none. Decision rule: Bayesian or regression adjustment. Data version: as of 2026-06-14. But note that due to label issues, this design is not feasible.
